name: Matter of Britain

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Matter of Britain, or Matiere de Bretagne, is a literary term. It describes the Arthurian legends that grew from presumed Celtic roots. The legends became part of the literary heritage of England. To a lesser extent they also shaped the heritage of France, and some Arthurian material is found in Celtic Brittany. The cycle includes Lancelot and Guinevere, the knights of the Round Table, the sorceress Morgan, and the magician Merlin. King Arthur himself crowns the cast. The Grail quest and a love triangle that destroys a heroic court are recurring motifs. Artists and authors drew inspiration from the Matter of Britain from medieval times onward. The Arthurian revival of the nineteenth century spread the figures and motifs of Camelot. Alfred Lord Tennyson wrote Idylls of the King. Mark Twain made Merlin a central figure in A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court. T. H. White wrote The Once and Future King and The Sword in the Stone. T. S. Eliot used the Grail figure of the Fisher King in The Waste Land. Marion Zimmer Bradley gave the tales a woman's viewpoint in The Mists of Avalon. The films include Excalibur by John Boorman.
objective: Document the Matter of Britain, the literary term for the Arthurian legends.
